newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German gold, French Left pose new EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: German gold, French Left pose new EMU doubts.

text.p: The German government and its fiercely independent central bank carried on with a war of words Friday as a power struggle over plans to revalue the nation's gold reserves cast fresh doubt over prospects for European monetary union.

Bonn's intention to revalue its official reserves has caused a political storm in Germany and, coupled with the likelihood of a leftist election win in France this weekend, poses serious question marks over future European economic integration.
If successful in Sunday's poll, French Socialists are likely to press for a broad monetary union with more countries, including Italy and Spain, involved from the start.
Economists, weighing the chances of an EMU delay, believe a broader EMU would water down the planned euro currency.
Markets, already nervous over the EMU implications of the German squabble and the French election, watched for signs of central banks stepping in to halt any fall in their currencies.
The mark jumped to a one-month high against the Italian lira, which was dented by a first-quarter dip in gross domestic product, seen as damaging Italy's EMU prospects.
Spain's budget secretary Jose Barea further stoked the EMU doubts, saying that Italy's high debts and budget deficit made it unlikely Rome could make the euro's starting line-up.
Theo Waigel, Germany's longest-serving finance minister, wants to revalue gold and foreign currency reserves to help plug gaps in state coffers pressured by near-record unemployment.

The Bundesbank, a leading crusader for a strong single currency, has condemned the move as damaging to the credibility of the planned euro and an affront to its independence from meddling politicians.

The revaluation, decried by many as an attempt by Bonn to cook the books and squeeze into monetary union in 1999, would involve the Bundesbank making special payments to Bonn in tranches in 1997 and 1998.
Germany books its gold at 144 marks per ounce against a market price of 600 marks. Revaluing these assets would bring the Bundesbank a windfall of 40 billion marks ($24 billion).
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke was reported as saying that one way out of the dispute would be for Bonn to drop a demand for a special profit payout after a gold revaluation.
Horst Siebert, a member of Bonn's economic advisory council known as the "five wise men," also warned that the revaluation plan threatened EMU's credibility.
"The whole plan is strongly impaired in its credibility and with it also the future (single) currency in its stability," Siebert told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper.
Siebert said it would be "reckless" to endanger foreign confidence in the Bundesbank, but added that strong reaction against the revaluation by the public and economists could force Bonn to back off.
But Peter Hintze, a top lieutenant of Chancellor Helmut Kohl, defended the plan and rejected calls for Waigel to quit.
The revaluation plan was economically and politically sensible, he told Deutschlandfunk radio, adding that the Bundesbank would eventually agree to the revaluation.
